AGENCY:
Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
Effective July 1, 2026, the U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) implemented certain changes to statistical reporting categories in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS). As a result of these changes, USTR is making a conforming amendment to an additional product exclusion associated with the Section 301 investigation of China's Acts, Policies, and Practices Related to Technology Transfer, Intellectual Property, and Innovation.
DATES:
The conforming amendment announced in the Annex to this notice is effective as of July 1, 2026. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will issue instructions on entry guidance and implementation.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For general questions about this notice, contact Philip Butler, Deputy Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Monitoring & Enforcement, or Rachel Hasandras, Assistant General Counsel, at (202) 395-5725. For specific questions on customs classification or implementation of the product exclusion identified in the Annex to this notice, contact
traderemedy@cbp.dhs.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
A. Background
Effective July 1, 2026, the USITC implemented certain changes to ten-digit statistical reporting categories of the HTSUS in accordance with its responsibility under section 484(f) of the Tariff Act of 1930, 19 U.S.C. 1484(f). Five of the product exclusions associated with the Section 301 investigation of China's Acts, Policies, and Practices Related to Technology Transfer, Intellectual Property, and Innovation, as set out in the Annexes at 89 FR 46948 (May 30, 2024), 90 FR 23987 (June 5, 2025), 90 FR 42500 (September 2, 2025), and 90 FR 55232 (December 1, 2025), were affected by the amended statistical reporting categories. On September 2, 2026, USTR issued a
Federal Register
notice with conforming amendments to four of the affected product exclusions. 91 FR 56538 (September 2, 2026).
( printed page 64212)
B. Conforming Amendment to Additional Product Exclusion
To maintain the pre-existing product coverage of the China 301 actions, a conforming amendment is required. The Annex to this notice makes a conforming amendment to U.S. note 20(vvv)(i)(20) to subchapter III of chapter 99 of the HTSUS, as set out in the Annexes at 89 FR 46948, 90 FR 23987, 90 FR 42500, and 90 FR 55232.
Annex
Effective with respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from the warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time on July 1, 2026, note 20(vvv)(i)(20) to subchapter III of chapter 99 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States is modified by inserting “through June 30, 2026; described in statistical reporting number 8479.90.9591 effective July 1, 2026” after “January 27, 2022.”
Jennifer Thornton,
General Counsel, Office of the United States Trade Representative.

high_priority_articles.summary: Japanese Yen softens as BoJ rate hike expectations recede, FOMC Minutes loom  FXStreet
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The USD/JPY pair gathers strength to around 158.35 during the early Asian trading hours on Wednesday. Receding expectations for a rate hike by the Bank of Japan (BoJ) weigh on the Japanese Yen (JPY) against the US Dollar (USD). Traders will closely monitor the Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) later on Wednesday.
BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Tuesday that the central bank would "assess the likelihood and risks of the baseline economic and price outlook being realized" when considering the pace and timing of future rate hikes. Market views that the Japanese central bank would take a cautious stance on rate increase at its October monetary policy meeting, weighing on the JPY.
The Bank of Japan's (BoJ) new policymaker Ayano Sato said that she supports the idea of raising interest rates in several stages, Reuters reported on Tuesday.
Pricing in overnight index swaps implies that markets see around a 12% odds of a rate hike this month, down from as high as 40% early last week, according to Bloombegr. The current probability surge to around 90% when the December meeting is included.
On the US’s front, traders reduce their bets on a Federal Reserve (Fed) rate hike this month following the softer-than-expected US jobs data. The US Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP) rose by 29K in September, compared to the 133K increase seen in August, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) showed on Friday. This figure came in below the market consensus of 90K. The Unemployment Rate climbed to 4.2% in September from 4.1% in August.
BoJ rate path seen as gradual as Fed tightening bets support elevated USD/JPY
Analysts at Rabobank note that, following the “as expected 25 bps rate rise last month,” market pricing now “suggests only a limited prospect of a policy move at the October 30 meeting, with expectations centring on December for the next policy move.” Even though BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated this morning that policymakers intend to “continue raising the policy interest rate” and described the Japanese economy as growing “moderately,” Rabobank argues that “this strengthens the market’s expectation that back-to-back rate hikes BoJ are unlikely.” As they put it, “even so, the Bank is still not widely viewed as being in a position in which back-to-back rate rises are appropriate,” although “this may suggest that a hastened pace of rate hikes is possible, though clearly that depends on how the economy develops in the months ahead.”
On the external side, Rabobank’s house view is that “the market has anticipated too much Fed policy tightening next year.” They contend that, “assuming some Fed rate hike risk is priced out, USD/JPY has the potential to move lower into 2027,” but for now “we maintain a 3-month USD/JPY target of 155.00.” While USD/JPY has moved higher since the September policy meeting, Rabobank highlights that “the market is fearful that a return to levels close to 160, could again trigger further intervention.” Against this backdrop, they judge that the BoJ’s inflation objective “now appears to have reached the point when it can instead shift its focus to stabilising price pressures around the target level,” reinforcing expectations for a measured, rather than aggressive, tightening path.
Fed’s schmid flags ai-driven inflation, keeps fed credibility and short-rate path in focus
Fed’s Schmid delivers a distinctly hawkish tone, with an 8/10 FXS Speechtracker score modestly above the 7.5/10 historical average, underscoring a firmer stance relative to the established baseline. The emphasis that inflation is “frustrating,” that the Fed “still has a way to go,” and that AI is now “one of the largest drivers of inflation” highlights concern about persistent price pressures and emerging structural forces, while the assertion that Fed credibility is at stake and that “the Fed still has work to do on the short rate despite higher long-term yields” signals a willingness to maintain or even tighten policy despite the bond market backdrop.
The FXS Fed Sentiment Index rose by 0.34 points to 137.91, reinforcing that the broader policy tone remains firmly in hawkish territory well above the neutral 100 threshold. This incremental uptick, aligned with the stronger-than-baseline speech score, suggests that Fed communication continues to support a resilient Dollar bias as markets price in a prolonged restrictive stance.
Technical Analysis: USD/JPY keeps a bearish vibe below the 100-day SMA
In the daily chart, USD/JPY remains capped in the near term, with the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) and the upper Bollinger Band forming overhead resistance that restrains recovery attempts. Price holds above the middle Bollinger Band, while the 14-day Relative Strength Index at 56.27 shows moderately constructive momentum that has yet to overcome the prevailing bearish structural bias set by the dominant longer-term average.
On the topside, initial resistance is located at the 100-day SMA at 159.55, followed by the upper Bollinger Band near 159.80. On the downside, immediate support sits at the middle Bollinger Band at 156.90, with a deeper cushion at the lower Bollinger Band around 154.00 should selling pressure reassert below the recent pivot at 158.38.

Japanese Yen FAQs
The Japanese Yen (JPY) is one of the world’s most traded currencies. Its value is broadly determined by the performance of the Japanese economy, but more specifically by the Bank of Japan’s policy, the differential between Japanese and US bond yields, or risk sentiment among traders, among other factors.
One of the Bank of Japan’s mandates is currency control, so its moves are key for the Yen. The BoJ has directly intervened in currency markets sometimes, generally to lower the value of the Yen, although it refrains from doing it often due to political concerns of its main trading partners. The BoJ ultra-loose monetary policy between 2013 and 2024 caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks. More recently, the gradually unwinding of this ultra-loose policy has given some support to the Yen.
Over the last decade, the BoJ’s stance of sticking to ultra-loose monetary policy has led to a widening policy divergence with other central banks, particularly with the US Federal Reserve. This supported a widening of the differential between the 10-year US and Japanese bonds, which favored the US Dollar against the Japanese Yen. The BoJ decision in 2024 to gradually abandon the ultra-loose policy, coupled with interest-rate cuts in other major central banks, is narrowing this differential.
The Japanese Yen is often seen as a safe-haven investment. This means that in times of market stress, investors are more likely to put their money in the Japanese currency due to its supposed reliability and stability. Turbulent times are likely to strengthen the Yen’s value against other currencies seen as more risky to invest in.

high_priority_articles.summary: The government must reach an agreement with the EU on postponing the CBAM for Ukraine — FRU  ЭкоПолитика
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Ukraine has every reason to expect the European Union to exempt it from the CBAM and to defer the introduction of the carbon levy. According to the business community, the full-scale war constitutes such an insurmountable circumstance, as it prevents the eco-modernisation of assets.
This was reported by RBC-Ukraine, citing a statement by Ruslan Illichov, Director-General of the Federation of Employers of Ukraine.
War constitutes a force majeure event
Under the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), the European Union requires importing countries to pay for embedded carbon emissions. For Ukrainian businesses, this pressure is insurmountable.
"We believe there are sufficient grounds for a force majeure to enable us to defer this payment," said Illichov during the United by Mining forum.
In his view, the full-scale war is preventing Ukrainian industry from meeting the European Union’s environmental requirements. These relate to reducing emissions in the production of metals and cement, and in the extraction of minerals.
In addition to the challenging military situation, steelmakers and cement producers will face further financial pressure following the introduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) on 1 January 2026, due to the need to pay a carbon duty when exporting their products to the EU.
What should I do?
The CEO of the FSU maintains that the Ukrainian government must now take proactive action. The task is to conduct productive negotiations with the European Commission.
A separate issue is that of default emission values. Where it is not possible to verify actual greenhouse gas emission levels, the EU applies default values to importers. According to Ruslan Illichov, these are too high for Ukrainian companies.
As a reminder, to verify emissions accreditors within the framework of the CBAM, Ukraine has agreed to receive assistance from the Swedish accreditation body SWEDAC.
In his first major interview, the new head of government mentioned that negotiations with the European Union regarding the CBAM for Ukraine are ongoing. The European Parliament has provisionally agreed to the possibility of applying special measures.
The European Parliament recently supported the extension of the scope of the CBAM to cover derivative goods manufactured from the main products, including fastenings and household items.

high_priority_articles.title: Fed policymakers saw multiple 2026 rate hikes as likely, September FOMC minutes show - Scotsman Guide
high_priority_articles.summary: Fed policymakers saw multiple 2026 rate hikes as likely, September FOMC minutes show  Scotsman Guide
high_priority_articles.full_text:
When Federal Reserve officials decided to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point in September, most also expected another rate hike before the end of 2026, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday.
“With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond the current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end,” the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) minutes read.
Meeting participants generally agreed that inflation remained too high, but differed over their rationales for the rate hike, the minutes show.
Some viewed September’s monetary tightening as a “risk management” cut, “providing insurance against inflation remaining persistently above target due to stronger-than-expected demand or further adverse supply shocks.”
Others emphasized that a higher policy rate would “help prevent sector-specific price increases stemming from energy market disruptions and AI-related demand from broadening out and generating more persistent inflation dynamics.”
And several participants “viewed the current policy rate as not restrictive or only mildly restrictive.”
But Fed staffers overshot the mark on their estimates of August inflation readings, predicting headline inflation measured by the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index would be 3.6% on a 12-month basis and core inflation less food and energy prices would be 3.2%.

Government data released two weeks after the Fed’s Sept. 16 rate decision showed headline PCE inflation at 3.4% and core inflation at 3%. Both figures were lower than consensus estimates, as economists polled by Reuters and Dow Jones had forecast overall annual growth of 3.7% and core gains of 3.3%.
October rate hike increasingly unlikely
Besides PCE inflation coming in below consensus, a weak September jobs report has bolstered the case for the Fed holding interest rates steady at the upcoming two-day FOMC meeting, which concludes Oct. 28. The central bank has a two-sided mandate to support stable prices and full employment.
U.S. employers added just 29,000 nonfarm jobs in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Oct. 2, landing well below consensus forecasts north of 80,000. The BLS also downwardly revised a combined 60,000 jobs from the prior two months’ payroll estimates.
Those data points have helped lower the odds of an October rate hike to just 17% as of Wednesday, according to CME FedWatch. The tool, which tracks futures contracts tied to the target range of the benchmark fed funds rate, puts the probability of a December hike at 84%.
Another reason for the anticipated rate hold: Midterm elections are looming in November.
While the Federal Reserve operates outside the political sphere, it has historically been careful to avoid the appearance of influencing the political narrative. When rate cuts or hikes have occurred just prior to a national election in the past, they have tended to be controversial.

Key Risk: Inflation prints re-accelerate and the Fed signals more hikes than expected, lifting real yields and crushing TIPS prices.
Buy the idea that the Fed stays hawkish into year-end: the minutes show “most participants” still see another hike as likely, and the pullback in October odds looks more like timing than a full pivot. Express via shorting 2-year Treasury futures (or buying 2Y yields).
Key Risk: October CPI/jobs come in hot enough to force a faster hike, pushing 2Y yields higher and breaking the “timing pullback” view.
- Fed officials saw a case for another rate hike by year-end.
- Markets now price only a 20% chance of an October Fed hike.
- Weaker jobs data could complicate the Fed’s October rate decision.
Federal Reserve officials broadly supported the central bank’s September interest-rate increase, with minutes showing that most policymakers saw a case for another hike by the end of the year as they assessed persistent inflation risks.
The minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee’s September 15-16 meeting, released Wednesday, showed that officials had different reasons for supporting the quarter-point increase.
Some viewed higher rates as necessary to limit the impact of energy and other price shocks, while others were more concerned about emerging demand-driven inflation.
“Most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end,” the minutes said.
The FOMC unanimously raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75% to 4% in September.
It was the first increase since July 2023 and came as officials saw signs of stronger economic momentum.
“Several participants commented that the underlying momentum in the economy appeared to have increased,” the minutes said.
Many policymakers also argued that another increase could provide insurance against inflation remaining above the Fed’s 2% target because of stronger-than-expected demand or additional supply shocks.
Markets scale back October hike bets
Despite the hawkish tone of the September minutes, expectations for an October rate increase have fallen sharply following more recent comments from Fed officials and weaker economic data.
Investors on Wednesday were pricing in roughly a 20% probability of a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting, down from around 70% in the days following the September decision, according to federal funds futures.
Two-year Treasury yields, which are particularly sensitive to expectations for Fed policy, had fallen more than 10 basis points over the previous week to around 4.76%.
Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams said last week that policymakers had time to assess the economy before deciding on another increase.
Their comments contributed to the pullback in expectations for an October hike.
The minutes also showed that several officials viewed the policy rate before the September increase as “not restrictive or only mildly restrictive.”
However, policymakers remain concerned about inflation.
Consumer price data due October 14 could influence the debate over whether another increase is needed this month.
Some officials who dissented in July in favour of a rate increase could potentially dissent again if the FOMC decides to leave rates unchanged in October.
Treasury yields and jobs remain in focus
The September meeting also included a discussion of financial conditions and the recent rise in longer-term Treasury yields.
Many officials said financial conditions remained supportive of economic growth, citing substantially higher equity prices and narrow corporate bond spreads.
Tom Graff, Chief Investment Officer at Facet, told Invezz that the minutes provided further support for his view that the Fed should raise rates at its October meeting.
Graff said the minutes showed limited concern about Treasury market volatility and suggested the Fed was unlikely to respond to bond-market moves in the near term.
The spike in long-term interest rates was also a topic of discussion. Based on some things he's said during his press conferences, Kevin Warsh views movement in longer-term rates in part as the market doing some of the Fed's tightening for them. It is hard to tell for sure from the minutes, but it doesn't seem to us that there's consensus about that. Based on the minutes there doesn’t seem to be great concern over Treasury market volatility, which in turn means there is little chance the Fed takes any action based on bond market activity in the near-term.
He noted that Treasury yields had risen amid higher oil prices and rising European yields, which he said reflected concerns over inflation and the potential for global rates contagion.
Graff added that volatility in the Treasury market may persist until there is greater stability.
The minutes described Treasury market functioning as “smooth,” but Graff said traders remained cautious. He expects investors to eventually look for opportunities in Treasury bonds, although he does not expect that to happen until the market shows signs of stability.
Graff also pointed to the labour market as a potential factor in the October decision.
"The labor market was described as 'stable,' but bear in mind this meeting occurred before the weaker September jobs report. It could be that when FOMC members get to the October meeting, there are more concerns over the labor market than was evident from these minutes." Graff added.
The combination of persistent inflation, softer labour data and elevated Treasury yields is likely to shape the debate over the Fed’s next policy move, with policymakers facing competing arguments over whether to raise rates again or wait for more economic data.

high_priority_articles.summary: Turkey to deploy troops and air defence systems to Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks  Middle East EyeTurkey sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia to help fight Houthis, officials say  ReutersWorld’s most powerful military and Africa avoids direct combat as Türkiye prepares to deploy troops and air defence systems to Saudi Arabia  Business Insider AfricaTurkey and Pakistan to send troops to support Saudi Arabia  The TimesTurkey prepares Saudi ...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Turkey plans to step up its military support for Saudi Arabia in the coming weeks by deploying additional personnel and defence equipment amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom, several Turkish officials told Middle East Eye on Tuesday.
In a joint statement on Monday, Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia said they had decided to immediately implement their collective defence commitments under the Makkah Alliance for Defence and provide "the agreed military forces and capabilities to ensure their rapid deployment" to the kingdom.
Two Turkish officials familiar with Ankara's plans told MEE that Turkey had maintained technical teams, air defence systems and electronic warfare equipment in the kingdom since last year to protect critical infrastructure, including energy facilities.
One senior Turkish official said Ankara would send additional equipment, technicians, emergency response teams and accompanying combat forces.
The official said a 2010 military training agreement between Saudi Arabia and Turkey allows Ankara to deploy limited forces to the kingdom for technical purposes. Further deployments, however, would require parliamentary authorisation under the Turkish constitution.
"We have to ratify the Makkah treaty as well but we may prioritise the military deployment authorisation bill," the official added.
A second Turkish official said Ankara planned to station military forces at at least one command base, solely to provide defensive support to Saudi Arabia.
"Technical teams carried out work in Saudi Arabia throughout September for the command base project, and preparations were nearing completion around the time the first Makkah Strategic Political and Defence Committee meeting was held," the official said.
The officials said a limited number of Turkish special forces could be deployed to the kingdom after the Turkish parliament approves a formal authorisation, which is expected later this month.
Separate sources familiar with the planning told MEE that, following parliamentary approval, the Turkish military would deploy an undisclosed number of experienced pilots and aircraft to Saudi Arabia to counter drones and ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis in Yemen.
"We don't plan to send a large group of soldiers and have no plans to directly intervene in Yemen," the senior Turkish official said.
"Ankara still believes diplomatic efforts might bear fruit in coming months."
Protect Riyadh, holy sites and major pipeline
The Turkish military is expected to help protect the western section of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and contribute to the defence of Riyadh and the holy cities.
Saudi sources told MEE that Turkish forces would operate alongside their Saudi and Pakistani counterparts at a joint coordination base, while the Turkish command unit would maintain a separate base of its own.
Turkish military personnel and technical defence support teams would be responsible for operations across multiple locations.
Murat Yesiltas, an academic and a member of Turkish Presidency's advisory board on foreign policy, said that Ankara would likely bring the Mecca Pact, or a deployment authorisation, to the Turkish Grand National Assembly's agenda within the next 30 days.
"Turkey's initial contribution, however, is far more likely to take the form of air defense, anti-drone systems, or intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) elements on Saudi Arabian soil, rather than deploying combat troops in Yemen," he wrote in a social media post.
"This approach allows Turkey to integrate into Riyadh's security network while simultaneously enabling it to controllably limit the level of risk and engagement it undertakes."
MEE was first to report in September that Turkey was preparing to provide defensive assistance to the kingdom while avoiding direct intervention inside Yemen.
For their part, the Houthis have denied trying to target the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, with the group's leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, calling the claims last month a "major lie."

high_priority_articles.title: Fed minutes: Another rate hike likely coming this year to combat persistent inflation - Yahoo Finance
high_priority_articles.summary: Fed minutes: Another rate hike likely coming this year to combat persistent inflation  Yahoo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, according to minutes released Wednesday from the central bank's most recent meeting.
The officials unanimously agreed that inflation was still elevated and had not made much progress toward their 2% target in recent months, the minutes said. The Fed increased its key interest rate at the Sept. 15-16 meeting by a quarter-point to about 3.9%, its first increase in three years.
The increase defied President Donald Trump's repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates and prompted the president to criticize the Fed's rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The rate increase comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries, gas and housing, and as affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away.
Longer-term interest rates for mortgages and other borrowing have also jumped in the past few months for a range of reasons, including rising government debt, heavy borrowing by tech firms to finance data center construction, climbing oil and gas prices, and signs that growth and inflation remain elevated. The Fed's rate hike has likely played only a limited role in the increase.
Still, key policymakers have said since the meeting that the Fed can take some time to monitor the economy and the impact of last month's rate hike before making another move. Wall Street investors now forecast the Fed will keep its rate unchanged at its next meeting Oct. 28-29, according to futures pricing, and raise it when they meet in December.
Philip Jefferson, vice chair of the Fed's board of governors, said last week that policymakers "will need to come to our own judgement, which may take more time."
Inflation, according to the Fed's preferred measure, came in lower than many economists expected in August but remained elevated. Overall prices rose 3.4% compared with a year earlier, while core prices — which exclude volatile food and energy categories — increased 3%. On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.3% from July to August, and core prices just 0.2%.
According to the minutes, even with the rise in longer-term rates, many officials said that financial conditions—which includes rising stock prices — "appeared to be supportive of economic growth," a sign that more rate hikes may be needed to cool the economy.

high_priority_articles.summary: Fed rate hike renews capital-flow, debt risks for emerging markets-INP  Independent News Pakistan
high_priority_articles.full_text:
By Qudsia Bano
The US Federal Reserve’s latest interest-rate increase has renewed concerns over capital outflows, higher borrowing costs and stronger dollar pressures across emerging markets, with economies carrying substantial foreign-currency debt particularly exposed to tighter global financial conditions.
The Federal Open Market Committee on September 16 raised the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 3.75-4.00%, reversing the easing trend seen in 2025. The Fed said inflation remained elevated and that the move would support a return towards its 2% objective.
The decision followed weeks of uncertainty over whether policymakers would tighten monetary policy or maintain rates at 3.50-3.75%.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller had highlighted that uncertainty earlier in September. In a September 3 speech, he said recent data were showing signs of disinflation and indicated that he would support keeping rates unchanged if subsequent inflation readings confirmed that improvement. However, he also left open the possibility of an increase if progress proved temporary.
The eventual rate increase has shifted attention from whether the Fed would tighten to how a renewed period of higher US rates could affect international financial conditions.
Speaking to Wealth Pakistan, Sakib Sherani, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Macro Economic Insights and former Principal Economic Adviser to the Ministry of Finance, said the implications of a fresh US monetary tightening cycle would extend across emerging markets rather than being confined to Pakistan.
“The start of a monetary tightening cycle in the US has deep implications for all emerging markets, not just Pakistan,” he said.
Sherani said that historically, rising US interest rates had encouraged what is known as a “flight-to-safety”, as investors moved risk capital away from emerging economies and towards US assets.
For countries such as Pakistan, he said, this transmission worked through two important channels: reduced availability of international private capital and appreciation of the US dollar.
“When the US Fed starts to raise interest rates, it accelerates the so-called ‘flight-to-safety’ phenomenon whereby risk capital starts to flow back from emerging markets to the US,” he said.
This shift, Sherani explained, reduces the pool of international private financing available to emerging economies and consequently raises their cost of accessing capital.
“It reduces the potential supply of international private capital, driving up the cost of capital,” Sherani said.
At the same time, higher US interest rates can support the dollar as investors seek higher returns in dollar-denominated assets. A stronger dollar can increase the domestic-currency burden of servicing foreign-currency liabilities.
Sherani said Fed tightening “strengthens the US dollar, which in turn makes the dollar-denominated sovereign debt of countries like Pakistan more expensive in revaluation terms.”
Pakistan remains sensitive to these external financial conditions because of its sizeable foreign-currency debt stock. According to the Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26, external public debt stood at $92.15 billion at end-March 2026, including $82.26 billion in government external debt and $9.89 billion owed to the International Monetary Fund.
The external debt portfolio also included $6.3 billion in Eurobonds and international Sukuk, exposing Pakistan to conditions in international capital markets when it seeks to refinance existing obligations or raise new commercial financing.
The impact of Fed tightening on Pakistan would therefore extend beyond movements in the policy rate itself. Higher US benchmark rates can increase the base cost of dollar financing before Pakistan’s own sovereign-risk premium is added, while shifts in international investor appetite can affect the availability of capital.
The September decision also does not necessarily establish how quickly or how far the Fed will tighten from here. The FOMC said economic activity was expanding at a solid pace, domestic spending remained resilient and inflation remained elevated, while uncertainty was still high partly because of geopolitical developments.
The Fed’s September projections also showed considerable differences among policymakers over the appropriate level of interest rates, underscoring uncertainty surrounding the future policy path.
The next scheduled FOMC meeting is on October 27-28, meaning incoming inflation, employment and economic activity data will again shape expectations over whether the September increase develops into a broader tightening cycle.
For Pakistan and other emerging economies, the significance therefore lies not simply in the Fed’s latest 25-basis-point increase but in what follows. As Sherani’s assessment suggests, a sustained US tightening cycle could reduce the availability of international private capital, raise external borrowing costs and increase the burden associated with dollar-denominated debt.
The September hike has consequently brought those risks back into focus, with the future direction of US inflation and Federal Reserve policy likely to remain important external variables for emerging-market financing conditions.

Drawing on the first comprehensive, firm-level study of its kind, this report presents empirical findings from an island-wide survey of 953 trading enterprises – capturing approximately 9% of all active importers and exporters in the country.

During last month’s 81st United Nations General Assembly, President Lee Jae-myung re-emphasized South Korea’s role as a Korean Peninsula pacemaker for peace. This follows his promise during last year’s first summit with U.S. President Donald Trump, where he asked Trump to be the ‘peacemaker’ while positioning himself as the pacemaker assisting him. However, looking at the recent actions of the South Korean government, there is growing concern that rather than becoming a pacemaker, it might turn into a ‘troublemaker’ causing confusion in the ROK-U.S. alliance and peace on the Korean Peninsula.
While covering the Aspen Security Forum last July, I had a conversation with a 25-year veteran foreign policy and security reporter who posed this question: ‘Wasn’t there a uniquely low level of mention regarding North Korea this year compared to last year?’
Looking back, that was indeed the case. While North Korea did appear when adversaries of the U.S. were discussed alongside China, Russia, and Iran, discussions dealing intensively with the direct threat of North Korea decreased noticeably. This contrasted sharply with last year, when North Korea’s cyber threats and other issues were treated as major agenda items. Even though North Korea continues to build its nuclear and missile capabilities and strengthen military cooperation with Russia, its presence in U.S. foreign policy discourse is fading.
Precisely because of this, the South Korean government must take action. It needs to inject agendas and capture attention within the U.S. Congress, executive branch, think tanks, and academia so that the North Korean nuclear issue, cyber threats, and human rights issues continue to be discussed. This is public diplomacy as well. Public diplomacy is not merely about promoting K-pop and K-food.
In particular, North Korean human rights are a crucial diplomatic leverage point that South Korea can utilize. In the U.S., North Korean human rights is treated as a bipartisan issue, as evidenced last June when Democratic Senator Tim Kimb and Republican Senator Dan Sullivan jointly sponsored a bill to reauthorize the North Korean Human Rights Act. Furthermore, U.S. law mandates a special envoy on North Korean human rights to raise international awareness of the severity of the situation. In the past, South Korea’s progressive administrations were criticized for placing North Korean human rights on the back burner in inter-Korean relations, and the current government is facing similar concerns. Even while pursuing dialogue with North Korea, the human rights issue of North Korean citizens must not be pushed to the margins of negotiations.
An even bigger problem is that at a time when North Korea-related agendas should be elevated in the U.S., diplomacy with Washington repeatedly displays scenes that amplify confusion rather than build trust. Recent discussions on U.S.-Korea investments are a prime example. When President Trump successively announced an $8.4 billion oil recovery project and an Alaska LNG investment, the South Korean government drew a line, stating the details were not agreed upon or required further review. The pattern of the U.S. president making announcements as if matters were finalized, only for the South Korean government to issue corrections, has repeated itself.
With this style of diplomacy toward the U.S., it is difficult for President Lee’s desired ‘pacemaker’ role to gain traction. Coordinating the pace between Washington and Pyongyang requires, above all, the trust of President Trump and Washington. If differing messages are sent even on trade and investment issues, how much would the U.S. trust South Korea if it claims to take on a mediating role in the much more sensitive North Korean nuclear negotiations? What a pacemaker needs is not a mere declaration, but diplomatic credibility that the counterpart can trust and rely upon.
The case of the past Moon Jae-in administration can serve as a counter-example. Back when inter-Korean and North Korea-U.S. summit diplomacy unfolded in 2018, former President Moon gained attention as a mediator. However, around the time of the 2019 Hanoi North Korea-U.S. summit, discontent arose in Washington over rushing the easing of sanctions. Furthermore, Pyongyang communicated directly with Trump, losing the need to go through South Korea. Having styled itself as a mediator, the very space for mediation vanished.
If President Lee genuinely wants to become a pacemaker for peace on the Korean Peninsula, he must straighten out the sequence. He must elevate the presence of the North Korean issue in the U.S., establish clear principles on the North Korean nuclear issue and human rights, and firmly solidify trust between South Korea and the United States first.
A pacemaker is not a position acquired simply by making a self-declaration. It is a role assumed only when the accompanying partner trusts you enough to entrust you with the pace. The pacemaker intended to lead peace on the Korean Peninsula must never become a troublemaker that tangles the flow.

South Africa is launching an ambitious new investment drive aimed at attracting R3 trillion (approximately US$181 billion) in investment between 2026 and 2030, as the country seeks to accelerate economic growth, modernise infrastructure, strengthen energy security and expand industrial capacity. The target follows a record R889.8 billion (approximately US$53.6 billion) in investment commitments secured at the sixth South Africa Investment Conference (SAIC) in March 2026, signalling a renewed focus on mobilising both domestic and international capital.
The latest investment drive comes at a critical point for the South African economy. While structural reforms have improved conditions in areas such as electricity supply and logistics, infrastructure constraints, high unemployment and relatively slow economic growth continue to limit the country's development potential.
The government is therefore positioning investment as a central mechanism for expanding productive capacity, creating jobs and attracting businesses into sectors with long-term growth potential. US$181 Billion Investment Ambition
The R3 trillion (US$181 billion) ambition represents the next phase of South Africa's investment mobilisation programme. According to government data, around R634 billion (US$38.2 billion) had actually flowed into the economy by March 2026, illustrating both progress and the challenge of converting commitments into completed projects.
The sixth SAIC provided a significant starting point for the new programme. The conference generated R889.8 billion (US$53.6 billion) in commitments across 81 projects, nine provinces and 22 source markets, with more than 230,000 permanent jobs expected from the announced projects. The commitments included R415 billion (US$25 billion) in confirmed fixed investment and R474.8 billion (US$28.6 billion) from development-finance institutions.
The government subsequently raised its ambition to R3 trillion (US$181 billion) for the 2026-2030 period. The scale of the target reflects the country's need for sustained investment rather than individual large projects.
Why Is South Africa Driving Investment?
South Africa's investment push is being driven by several structural priorities. One of the most important is the need to close infrastructure gaps that have constrained economic activity.
The government estimates that public-sector infrastructure expenditure will reach approximately R1.07 trillion (US$64.5 billion) over the next three years. Planned spending includes electricity, roads, rail, ports, water and other strategic infrastructure.
Energy security is another major priority. South Africa has historically faced electricity shortages, although reforms and additional generation have substantially improved reliability. The government says regulatory changes have helped unlock a renewable-energy pipeline exceeding 220 GW, with approximately 36 GW already in the grid-connection process.
Transport infrastructure is equally important. SANRAL plans investment of approximately R300 billion to R400 billion (US$18.1 billion-US$24.1 billion) in national roads and strategic freight corridors, while Transnet has identified up to R250 billion (US$15.1 billion) for ports and logistics modernisation.
The broader objective is to reduce the cost of doing business, improve connectivity and create the infrastructure required for manufacturing, mining and exports.

Energy Investment
Energy is expected to remain one of the largest investment opportunities. South Africa is seeking to expand renewable generation while upgrading transmission infrastructure and developing energy-storage capacity.
The country's renewable-energy pipeline provides opportunities for developers, engineering companies, equipment manufacturers, battery-storage providers, transmission specialists and financial institutions.
The government has also identified approximately 14,000 kilometres of new transmission lines, with an estimated cost of around R450 billion (US$27.1 billion), as a major investment opportunity. A Credit Guarantee Vehicle is being developed to reduce investor risk and attract private capital into transmission projects.
The energy transition is also opening opportunities in green hydrogen, battery storage, electric vehicles and renewable-energy component manufacturing. At the 2026 Investment Conference, confirmed renewable-energy investment amounted to approximately R29 billion (US$1.75 billion), reflecting growing private-sector participation in the sector.
For businesses, the opportunity extends beyond electricity generation. Transmission, grid management, energy storage, engineering, maintenance and local manufacturing could become important areas of long-term growth.

Mining remains another pillar of South Africa's investment strategy. The country possesses substantial reserves of minerals that are increasingly important to global energy and technology supply chains.
South Africa's deposits of platinum-group metals, manganese, chromium and other critical minerals provide opportunities to move beyond raw-material extraction toward processing and manufacturing.
The government is placing greater emphasis on mining beneficiation, which means increasing the amount of processing and value addition that takes place domestically. This could create opportunities for processing plants, mineral-refining technologies, specialised equipment, logistics companies and manufacturers using locally processed materials.

Developing domestic value chains could allow South Africa to capture a larger share of the economic value generated by its mineral resources.

Infrastructure development is likely to generate opportunities across construction, engineering, logistics, telecommunications, water and transport.
South Africa's infrastructure financing requirement is particularly large. This means government budgets alone cannot meet the country's infrastructure requirements and private investment will have to play a much larger role.
The opportunity therefore extends to infrastructure funds, pension funds, banks, private-equity investors, construction companies and international engineering firms.
Ports and rail are especially important because South Africa's mining and manufacturing sectors depend heavily on efficient freight networks. Improving these systems could reduce bottlenecks and strengthen the country's role as a gateway for regional trade.

high_priority_articles.summary: Fed Minutes Show Unanimous Support for September Rate Hike as Officials Weigh Another Increase  IndexBox
high_priority_articles.full_text:
According to meeting minutes made public on Wednesday, every one of the 19 Federal Reserve officials endorsed the quarter-point boost to the benchmark interest rate decided late last month, pointing to a steady economy and labor market while stressing the need to bring inflation down to the Fed's 2% target.
The Sept. 28 move, which the 12 Federal Open Market Committee policymakers approved without dissent, additionally received backing from the seven regional bank presidents who serve on the FOMC on a rotating basis but are not presently committee members, the minutes showed.
Most participants judged that a further rise in the target range for the federal funds rate would probably be warranted before the year was out, the minutes said. Participants stressed, though, that they came to every meeting with an open mind and that choices at upcoming meetings would hinge on fresh information.
Since the Sept. 28 FOMC decision, two senior policymakers -- Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams -- have signaled they feel no urgency about raising borrowing costs, a view strengthened Friday by data showing weak job gains.
The Labor Department reported that the U.S. added only 29,000 jobs in September, below forecasts, while July and August combined were revised down by 60,000 positions from earlier figures. The unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%, 0.1 percentage point above August's level.
Sluggish hiring and the gentler stance on combating inflation taken by Jefferson and Williams led interest rate futures traders to cut the probability that the Fed will lift the main rate this month to 17.2% from 37.6% a week earlier, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.
The central bank aims to keep inflation at 2% but has not managed to hit that mark for over five years. Although most Fed officials last month projected one additional hike in the main rate this year, a handful signaled they expect two more.
During the September FOMC meeting, Fed officials raised concerns about climbing inflation expectations, the minutes showed. Some participants worried that, with inflation above 2% for more than five years, elevated rates could start to influence inflation expectations as well as decisions on wages and prices.
Central bank officials monitor inflation expectations closely, since they believe such views can turn self-fulfilling. As a result, growing household expectations of higher price pressures support tighter monetary policy.

high_priority_articles.title: France fires upgraded nuclear-capable missile from submarine for first time - Defense News
high_priority_articles.summary: France fires upgraded nuclear-capable missile from submarine for first time  Defense NewsFrance completes test of new nuclear-capable missile  Le Monde.frKremlin Says France's Test Nuclear Launch Is Part of 'Dead End' Anti-Russia Strategy  The Moscow TimesFrance tests upgraded nuclear missile against backdrop of Russia tensions  ReutersUkraine war live: Kremlin responds to France testing upgraded nuclear weapon  The Independent
high_priority_articles.full_text:
PARIS — France test-fired an upgraded version of its M51 strategic ballistic missile from a submarine for the first time on Tuesday, a capability demonstration that President Emmanuel Macron called “very important” for the country’s strategic credibility and which he said would be monitored by allies and adversaries alike.
The nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine Le Vigilant fired an M51.3 missile in an acceptance test following the boat’s overhaul, the Ministry of the Armed Forces said in a statement. The missile, which didn’t carry a nuclear warhead, was launched off Finistère in western France and splashed down in the North Atlantic several hundred kilometers from any coastline, the ministry said.
France’s work to upgrade the M51 missile, manufactured by ArianeGroup, is part of a broader modernization of the country’s nuclear deterrence apparatus that also includes the construction of new ballistic-missile submarines and a future upgrade of the Rafale fighter jet that would carry a hypersonic nuclear cruise missile.
“This is a very important moment for our strategic credibility,” Macron told troops onboard a French Navy vessel from which he observed the launch. “Everything that has happened recently and what is happening today will be closely scrutinized by both our allies and our competitors alike, and it already is. Along the course we have set, this is a step forward.”
The modernization of France’s nuclear arsenal comes as the country works with several European allies on what Macron has called “forward deterrence,” a proposal that could involve extending the reach of French nuclear deterrence to those allies, although the details of what that would look like remain vague for now.
Every major overhaul of a French nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine is followed by an acceptance test firing of the M51, the ministry told Defense News in an emailed response to questions.
ArianeGroup and France’s Directorate General for Armament completed a first flight test of the modernized M51 from a launch site in Biscarrosse in southwest France in 2023, and the new missile entered operational service in October last year.
The latest M51.3 variant is estimated to have a range of more than 9,500 kilometers, from more than 9,000 kilometers for the previous version, according to the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. The missile carries four to six multiple independently-targetable reentry vehicles, or MIRVs, according to the Bulletin.
While the official range of the missile is undisclosed, ArianeGroup says the M51 reaches an altitude of more than 2,000 kilometers before reentering the atmosphere at a speed of Mach 20.
The missile is equipped with the new TNO-2 oceanic nuclear warhead, and offers better performance in terms of range, accuracy and penetration capability, according to the ministry. The solid-propellant three-stage missile weighs more than 50 metric tons, and each of France’s four ballistic missile submarines can carry 16 of them.
“The M51.3 ensures the long-term credibility of the ocean-based component in the face of evolving adversary missile defenses,” the ministry said. “It reflects the commitment of the President of the Republic to maintaining operational credibility of the nuclear forces over the long term, at the level required by the international environment.”
The first version of the M51 was fired from the Biscarrosse launch site in 2006, with the first submarine launch from the SSBN Le Terrible in January 2010. Today’s launch was the seventh time a variant of the M51 was fired from a French submarine, and the 13th launch of the missile overall, all of them “of course, conducted without a nuclear warhead,” according to the ministry.
Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

high_priority_articles.summary: India-US Trade Talks Stall as Tariff Risks Intensify  Serrari Group
high_priority_articles.full_text:

India-US trade negotiations have reached a difficult stage, with Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman saying the two sides have reached a point where further concessions are increasingly difficult.
The stalemate comes despite more than a year of negotiations and a trade framework announced earlier in 2026. New US tariff powers linked to purchases of Russian energy have complicated the negotiations further, leaving India balancing access to its largest export market against energy-security considerations and domestic economic pressures.
Both governments say negotiations are continuing, but officials on both sides have publicly signalled that a final agreement is not imminent.
Key Overview
- India says trade negotiations with the US have reached a “plateau”, leaving limited space for further concessions.
- The two countries have been negotiating a bilateral trade agreement since 2025.
- A February 2026 framework lowered punitive US tariffs on many Indian products, but a final comprehensive agreement remains unfinished.
- New US legislation allows tariffs of up to 100% on qualifying major buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas.
- India remains one of the largest purchasers of Russian oil, making energy policy a major factor in the trade negotiations.
- The US remains India’s largest export destination, with merchandise exports reaching $42.79 billion between April and August 2026.
Negotiations Reach a Difficult Stage
Sitharaman offered one of New Delhi’s clearest acknowledgements yet that the negotiations are struggling, saying trade talks have reached a plateau while stressing that discussions are continuing.
Her comments followed a similar signal from Washington. After discussions with Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that although negotiators had identified the remaining sticking points, a final agreement was not imminent and further work was still required.
The current difficulties follow substantial progress earlier in the year. The two countries announced a trade framework in February 2026 aimed at reducing tariff and non-tariff barriers and deepening bilateral commerce.
That framework lowered punitive tariffs on most Indian goods from 50% to 18%, although subsequent US legal and trade-policy changes altered the tariff environment again.
The negotiations nevertheless remain focused on longstanding issues including market access, agricultural products, tariff certainty and the bilateral trade imbalance.

Russian Oil Adds a New Trade Complication
The biggest new uncertainty comes from US legislation targeting countries that continue purchasing Russian energy.
A law enacted on September 18 gives the US president authority to impose duties of up to 100% on goods from countries meeting defined criteria related to Russian crude oil or natural-gas purchases and sanctions evasion.
The measure focuses in part on countries ranking among the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas. India’s continued purchases therefore create a potentially significant source of trade risk.
For New Delhi, the calculation is complicated. India relies heavily on imported energy and has purchased substantial volumes of discounted Russian crude since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
A sharp reduction in those supplies could increase procurement costs and place pressure on domestic fuel prices or public finances. Continuing large purchases, however, exposes Indian exporters to the possibility of significantly higher US tariffs.
The legislation provides scope for adjustments and waivers, meaning the maximum tariff is not automatically imposed simply because a country buys Russian energy. Even so, the additional authority has increased uncertainty around the final tariff treatment India could secure through a bilateral trade agreement.
Trade With the US Remains Crucial for India
The stakes are significant because the United States remains India’s largest individual export market.
Indian goods exports to the US reached $42.79 billion during April-August 2026, up from just over $40 billion during the comparable period a year earlier.
India’s wider export performance has also remained strong. Official figures show total merchandise exports reached $215.91 billion during April-August, representing growth of 17.85% from the previous year.
The large US market is especially important for sectors including pharmaceuticals, electronics, engineering goods, textiles and other manufactured products. This makes tariff certainty one of New Delhi’s main objectives in the negotiations.
Washington, meanwhile, has repeatedly highlighted the US trade deficit with India and is seeking greater access to the Indian market.
Agriculture and Tariff Certainty Remain Sticking Points
Agriculture remains among India’s most politically sensitive negotiating areas. New Delhi has sought to shield products including dairy, poultry, wheat and rice from broad market-opening commitments while pressing for more predictable US tariff treatment.
Washington is also conducting a Section 301 investigation into industrial overcapacity covering India and several other economies, creating another source of uncertainty over future tariff levels.
This leaves both sides with limited room to make further concessions. India wants stronger guarantees over market access before committing to deeper liberalisation, while Washington is seeking movement on trade barriers, Russian energy purchases and the bilateral imbalance.
The negotiations therefore remain active but increasingly constrained. A final agreement would strengthen one of the world’s largest bilateral trading relationships, but the combination of energy security, domestic political sensitivities and new tariff powers means reaching the remaining compromises could prove more difficult than the progress already achieved.

high_priority_articles.summary: Vietnam finalises proposal to sign free trade agreement with EFTA  Fibre2Fashion
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Negotiations on VEFTA began in 2012, and the two sides have concluded discussions on the full text after more than 14 years and 21 official negotiating rounds, according to the Ministry of Industry and Trade.
The proposed agreement is expected to widen market access for Vietnamese exporters in high-purchasing-power markets. The ministry said EFTA members have committed to immediately liberalising more than 90 per cent of tariff lines, covering 99.5 per cent of Vietnam’s exports to the bloc.
EFTA would also remove tariffs immediately on all industrial products, including seafood. Major Vietnamese export categories set to benefit from immediate tariff elimination include textiles and garments, footwear, seafood, computers, electronic products and components, machinery and equipment.
The agreement also provides for tariff reductions by EFTA on a number of major Vietnamese agricultural products, including rice, honey, fruits and vegetables. Vietnam, for its part, has offered to eliminate tariffs on more than 86 per cent of tariff lines, equivalent to 99.9 per cent of imports from EFTA, either immediately or under reduction schedules ranging from three to 15 years.
The proposed deal covers trade in goods and services, investment, rules of origin, technical barriers to trade, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, trade facilitation, government procurement, intellectual property, competition, small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), and sustainable development.
Vietnamese exports to EFTA markets with good turnover and growth in 2024-2025 included seafood at more than $52 million, footwear at more than $49 million, computers, electronic products and components at more than $40 million, and textiles and garments at more than $26 million. Other export categories included machinery, equipment, tools and spare parts, and means of transport.
Vietnam mainly imports from EFTA products serving domestic production, including machinery and equipment, electrical and mechanical products, chemicals, seafood materials and pharmaceuticals, as reported by a govt news portal.
In investment cooperation, Switzerland and Norway are the EFTA members with significant ties to Vietnam. As of the end of 2025, Switzerland had 234 valid investment projects in Vietnam with total registered capital of more than $2.4 billion, ranking 20th among 153 countries and territories investing in the country. Norway had 62 valid projects with registered capital of $201.57 million, ranking 40th.
The ministry said signing the agreement is expected to help Vietnamese enterprises diversify export markets and improve access for Vietnamese goods to markets with high purchasing power and stringent quality standards. EFTA’s annual import turnover is around $630 billion, while imports from Vietnam currently account for about 0.65 per cent, indicating room for further growth.
The agreement is also expected to attract high-quality investment from EFTA countries into sectors prioritised by Vietnam, including high technology, processing and manufacturing, clean energy, green transition, innovation and human resource development.
EFTA comprises Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
By XING YI in London | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-10-07 22:56
Ahead of high-level trade talks between China and the European Union later this week, Chinese officials and experts have warned France and Germany against resorting to protectionist measures, politicizing economic issues and framing them in terms of security.
The warning came after a letter jointly signed by French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to bolster the EU with a new trade diversification instrument and a new trade defense measure.
Reuters reported on Monday that the letter, together with an unofficial proposal paper, had been welcomed by the commission, which said it was a valuable contribution to the debate on geoeconomic risks and global imbalances, and aligned with Von der Leyen's stance on competitiveness and her approach to EU trading partners.
Though the letter did not mention China, analysts said China was the most likely focus of the proposal as it was sent out before possible China-EU trade talks on Thursday.
A spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday that the ministry had taken note of the report and expressed hope that France and Germany, as major global economies, would uphold openness, cooperation and free trade, abide by World Trade Organization rules, and refrain from encouraging the EU to resort to protectionist measures at every turn. Still less should they politicize economic and trade issues under the garb of security concerns.
"They should avoid taking the wrong approach down the wrong path, which could ultimately backfire on themselves," the spokesperson said.
The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU also issued a response opposing the reported proposal in its current form and calling for continued dialogue, consultation and a balanced approach to addressing trade concerns.
"At a particularly critical stage of the ongoing China-EU trade negotiations, we believe that introducing such a mechanism could increase uncertainty, undermine mutual trust and complicate efforts to achieve constructive and tangible outcomes," said a spokesperson for the CCCEU.
In June, China and the EU held the first round of trade talks and established four workstreams covering trade and investment balancing, export controls, intellectual property rights and WTO reform.
The progress came against the backdrop of deep economic ties between the two sides, with bilateral trade exceeding $828 billion in 2025.
Michael Schumann, chairman of the board of the Federal Association for Economic Development and Foreign Trade of Germany, said German businesses are increasingly concerned about the political uncertainty surrounding the economic relationship between the two sides and expect a credible political signal that the EU and China want to manage their differences rather than escalate them.
"Companies need predictability," said Schumann. They want fair competition and better market access, and want to preserve the enormous opportunities that continue to exist in China, he added.
"At the same time, Europe should avoid creating the impression that new economic instruments are an end in themselves. Strong instruments can have a role as a safeguard and as leverage in negotiations, but the objective must always be to create better and more balanced conditions for trade."
He said the logic that every dispute must be answered with another restriction should be avoided. "Once retaliation becomes the dominant dynamic, businesses and consumers on both sides lose."
Schumann regarded the talk of a "kill switch" in the current debate and reporting surrounding the Franco-German paper as irresponsible rhetoric.
"I have said repeatedly that language matters in international relations. Words can open doors, but they can also close them. Europe should defend its legitimate economic interests firmly, but we should not talk ourselves into a confrontation that neither side can benefit from," he added.
Mark Logan, a London-based political risk consultant and former member of the British Parliament, said Europe should pay close attention to signs of greater engagement displayed at the recent China-United States summit and pursue more cooperation with China rather than engage in protectionist measures.
"European leaders must find a way to work with China and the new emerging centers of economic power by learning the most important ingredients for their success: technological innovation and entrepreneurialism," said Logan.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
South Korean activists campaigning for workplace safety in the nation's booming semiconductor industry called on the government on Wednesday to recognise the cancer diagnoses of three former SK hynix employees as work-related illnesses.
SK hynix, along with fellow South Korean tech giant Samsung Electronics, has emerged as a key player in the booming artificial intelligence industry, with its cutting-edge memory chips crucial to powering the sector's rapid growth.
Establishing direct links between semiconductor work and certain cancers can be contentious, with research inconclusive. But fabrication and assembly plant workers can face exposure to solvents, acids, toxic metals and chemical gases, according to the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
Samsung issued a public apology in 2018 to workers -- many of them young women -- who had developed cancer after working at some of its factories, paying out 150 million won per case (about $130,000 at the time) after a decade-long dispute.
Supporters for the Health and Rights of People in the Semiconductor Industry (SHARPS) , one of the groups that had pressured Samsung, said on Wednesday chemicals classified as carcinogens were being used by SK hynix.
"We have confirmed that several substances on SK hynix's own list of prohibited chemicals are in fact being used, including nickel and its compounds," Lee Sang-soo, a SHARPS activist, told a news conference, citing data reported by SK hynix to the environment ministry.
SK hynix said in a statement sent to AFP it was "taking various measures to more objectively identify the characteristics of disease occurrence" and was fully cooperating with government inquiries.
The company, which did not address the specific claims, said it had taken "proactive industrial health measures including the development of a comprehensive support and compensation plan".
The husband of a former SK hynix worker who died from breast cancer called on the Korea Workers' Compensation & Welfare Service to recognise his wife's illness as work-related.
"I believe the nature of her job meant that she was inevitably exposed to various hazardous substances," Kim Yong-il, the husband of Yoon Young-mi, told the briefing outside the offices of the service, which is a government agency.
Yoon began working at SK hynix's Icheon chip plant in 1996 and was diagnosed with cancer in 2018. She died in April.
"The company and the relevant authorities must protect workers' right to health when it comes to occupational diseases in the semiconductor industry," Kim said.
Agency representative Ko Seong-yong of the Korea Workers' Compensation & Welfare Service told AFP that authorities would "process their cases as fast as possible".
"An epidemiological investigation is necessary. While it is difficult to give an exact timeframe, it could take around a year before a decision is made," he said.
