E3T Unit 2, a space verification satellite developed by Nara Space Technology (Nara Space), succeeded in two-way communication with the ground station after the fifth launch of Nuri. The satellite will verify in the actual space environment the performance of devices and parts developed in Korea, including SK hynix memory semiconductors onboard.
Nara Space said on the 8th that E3T Unit 2 was launched aboard Nuri at 12:25 p.m. on the 7th from the Naro Space Center in Goheung, South Jeolla, and communicated normally with the ground station.
E3T Unit 2 separated from Nuri about 17 minutes after liftoff and succeeded in its first two-way communication with the Nara Space satellite control center about 1 hour and 57 minutes later. It is currently conducting initial operations to check the satellite's basic status and key functions.
E3T Unit 2 is a 12U (1U is 10 cm in width, length, and height) class cubesat designed to test domestically developed semiconductors, electronic devices, and satellite parts in the actual space environment. It weighs about 18 kg, and Nara Space handled development of the satellite platform bus and post-launch operations.
The satellite carries SK hynix memory semiconductors, Inserasolution's high-speed precision steering mirror, Momentum Space's reaction wheel, and KAIST's attitude determination and system module. Cosmovy's hollow cathode for electric thrusters and Intergravity Technologies' avionics for an orbital transfer vehicle will also have their performance tested in space.
After completing initial orbital operations, E3T Unit 2 will begin full-scale verification missions. It will repeatedly operate the payloads, downlink data to the ground, and check how space radiation and large temperature swings affect the operation of devices and parts.
The satellite was developed under the Korea AeroSpace Administration's "domestically made device and part space verification support project." The Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) is in charge of program management and satellite system integration, and Nara Space handled the platform development and operations for Unit 2 following E3T Unit 1, which flew on the fourth Nuri launch last year.
Since its launch in Nov. last year, E3T Unit 1 has been carrying out missions to verify in the space environment domestically made devices and parts such as Samsung Electronics memory semiconductors and KAIST integrated circuits.
Park Jae-pil, CEO of Nara Space, said, "We will continue to keep pace with the global new space trend to expand verification opportunities for various space-grade devices and parts, and steadily build related capabilities so we can serve as a foundation for the growth of the domestic space device and parts industry."

high_priority_articles.title: Russia’s Hybrid War Has Entered a Dangerous New Phase
high_priority_articles.summary: Julianne Smith, who represented the United States at NATO during the Biden administration, argues that Russian hybrid warfare in Europe is escalating quickly, and NATO is not doing enough to deter it. Putin is attempting to discourage support for Ukraine and undermine faith in Article 5, and NATO is responding with an outdated playbook.
high_priority_articles.full_text:
For the first few years of the war in Ukraine, Russia’s hybrid warfare attacks in Europe remained just below the threshold that might trigger a collective response. As the United States’ permanent representative to NATO from 2021 to 2024, I watched the campaign develop: undersea cables cut, incendiary devices hidden in cargo packages, and arson attacks on weapons factories and depots across Europe. To address the threat, allies reinforced critical infrastructure, increased patrols in the Baltic Sea, and expanded intelligence sharing. But NATO’s approach remained largely defensive: these attacks were scattered, small in scale, and just deniable enough that Moscow could wave them away.
Today, that is no longer the case. In late July, a Russian cruise missile crashed into Polish territory. Days later, three explosive-laden drones were found at and near an airport in Leipzig, Germany. Two weeks after that, Romanian F-16s scrambled to intercept three Russian drones over Romanian airspace, and a Spanish jet shot down a fourth near the Moldovan border. If someone had described this state of affairs two years ago as where NATO would be now—drones over allied airspace, a Russian cruise missile in Polish territory, explosives at a German airport—without any meaningful collective response from the alliance, it would have sounded unbelievable.
There is little ambiguity about Russian President Vladimir Putin’s aims. These attacks are designed to fracture the alliance’s unity, test the strength of members’ commitment to Article 5—the principle that an attack on one member is an attack on all—and raise the cost of supporting Ukraine. Less expected, however, has been the speed with which his deniable campaign has become undeniable.
NATO has not looked away. The alliance tracks these incidents, investigates them, and sometimes intercepts attacks. But a response built incident by incident is not deterrence, and Putin knows the difference. As long as each provocation costs Moscow nothing more than a downed drone, Putin has every reason to keep escalating. And every escalation in turn increases the risk that one of these incidents will end in catastrophic loss of life. Mobilizing collective action to impose costs is the best chance the alliance has of preventing such a scenario.
MASK OFF
For Russia, hybrid tactics are far from a new tradecraft. As early as the 1920s and continuing throughout the Cold War, the Soviets relied on what they called “active measures”: the use of local proxies, front groups, and irregular forces to achieve political aims. Today, Putin follows essentially the same model, seeking to erode allies’ confidence in NATO’s Article 5 by relying on tactics that fall below the threshold of a conventional warfare and leave unaffected members hesitant to respond. Plausible deniability has always been a critical part of these operations. Whatever the method, whether it be severing undersea fiber-optic cables in the Baltic Sea, a coordinated cyberattack, or an explosion at a plant in eastern Europe that produces artillery shells for Ukraine, Russia is quick to deny its direct involvement. Often, it flips the script, accusing NATO members of “Russophobia” and directing blame at Ukrainian or rogue actors.
NATO members have long been familiar with this Russian playbook. Most European members have experienced multiple hybrid attacks over the past two decades. But since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has changed its strategy in two meaningful ways. First, it has significantly increased the frequency of attacks; during the first year of the war, the number of Russian incursions in Europe quadrupled, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. It has also diversified its tactics. In addition to familiar disinformation campaigns, airspace violations, and cyberattacks, actors linked to Moscow have sabotaged railways, placed incendiary packages on cargo planes, and paid criminal networks inside Europe to burn down weapons depots.
By early 2023, in response to these trends, NATO stepped up the seriousness and urgency of its discussions on Russian hybrid activity. The 2023 NATO summit’s communiqué, which sets out the alliance’s shared positions and priorities, stated that Russia had “intensified” its attacks against allies and mentioned Russia’s use of proxies for the first time. The alliance also rolled out an array of new initiatives to counter hybrid activity: heads of state adopted new goals for protecting critical infrastructure and supply chains from strategic shocks across alliance territory. They also agreed to establish the NATO Maritime Centre for the Security of Critical Undersea Infrastructure and the Virtual Cyber Incident Support Capability, a coordination platform to help members respond to cyberattacks. What was missing was any measure to impose costs on Russia. Although NATO condemned Moscow’s hybrid warfare, it was not prepared to talk explicitly about consequences, such as targeted sanctions, a crackdown on Russia’s shadow fleet (the unmarked vessels Russia uses to bypass sanctions), offensive cyber-activities, or information operations.
 In late 2025, Putin put his hybrid war into overdrive. 
Part of the problem is structural. NATO was established and designed, in 1949, for collective defense against attributable armed attacks. It was not designed to impose costs after deniable acts. As a defensive military alliance, it lacks the authority to impose sanctions or expel Russian operatives from member countries. That power sits with individual member states and the European Union. Since its 2014 summit, NATO has maintained that a cyber or hybrid attack could trigger Article 5 on a “case by case basis,” but the alliance has never defined the threshold for action. Even in cases in which the alliance could act collectively, such as through offensive cyber-operations, doing so requires consensus among 32 countries that have very different histories, domestic politics, and appetites for risk.
In the year after the 2023 NATO summit, Russia continued to turn up the heat, tripling its hybrid attacks in Europe and testing new ways to target NATO territory, such as interference with European railway systems. Consequently, the alliance improved its detection, forensics, and response options. NATO members shared best practices, participated in tabletop exercises designed to test those options, and crafted a new strategy to counter disinformation. Many countries, such as Estonia, Germany, Poland, and the United Kingdom, independently opened investigations into, sought prosecutions of, and expelled Russian diplomats and suspected intelligence officers. These steps were important. But they were not enough to deter Russia.
In 2025, hopes for further NATO action stalled. When President Donald Trump returned to the White House, he was so intent on getting NATO members to spend more on defense that virtually every engagement with allies began and ended with that single issue. Such ruthless prioritization produced some admirable results. At the 2025 NATO summit at The Hague, all allies committed to spend five percent of GDP on defense by 2035. But instead of taking the win and directing the alliance’s attention back toward Russia’s hybrid warfare, the administration continued to badger allies to spend more and faster. When I visited NATO headquarters in November 2025 and asked former colleagues how they were spending their time, one country’s permanent representative answered, “We spend most of our time managing you.” Amid this upheaval, the alliance’s momentum on hybrid warfare slowed to a crawl. Despite an agreement among allies in 2024 to deliver a new Russia strategy at the 2025 summit at The Hague, it never materialized. The summit declaration didn’t even mention Russia’s hybrid war.
FROG IN A POT
The summer of 2025 seemed to mark a high point for Putin’s confidence. In addition to NATO’s waning focus on hybrid activity, Russia’s summer offensive in Ukraine was showing signs of success, NATO allies were bickering over tariffs and whether Europe was facing what Vice President JD Vance called “civilizational suicide,” and Putin was being courted by Trump, a dynamic on public display in a U.S.-Russian summit in Alaska in August.
By September 2025, Putin no longer seemed to care as much about plausible deniability, and Russia’s hybrid war campaign became increasingly brazen. That month, around 20 Russian drones entered Polish airspace, and three Russian fighter jets crossed into Estonian airspace before being shot down and chased out, respectively, by NATO forces. After each instance, NATO convened for Article 4 consultations, which, according to the treaty, take place when “the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the Parties is threatened.” NATO launched “Eastern Sentry,” an initiative to increase NATO’s vigilance over the alliance’s eastern flank with no set end date. The initiative placed additional allied air and counterdrone assets under NATO command to reinforce its existing integrated air and missile defense along that border. Although a much-needed addition to NATO’s efforts to combat hybrid warfare, this step also failed to deter Russian attacks.
 NATO needs to mount a more forceful response to Moscow’s escalation.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
India's first bank rate hike since 2023 signals growing inflation concerns
Indians may have to pay more for car, home and personal loans after the federal bank raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in nearly four years in a bid to rein in inflation.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced a 25 basis points increase in its repo rate to 5.5% - this is the rate at which it lends money to commercial banks which then pass on the additional cost to customers.
Federal banks across the world have adopted tighter monetary policy amid energy-driven inflation as the war in the Middle East continues.
India's benchmark equity indices Sensex and Nifty fell with investors weighing the implications of higher borrowing costs for consumption and corporate investment.
In his post-policy address, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said the decision reflected challenging geopolitical developments, even as the Indian economy remained strong.
He said cuts were "off the table for now", with the central bank likely to either raise rates further or keep them unchanged to contain inflation.
The RBI projects Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation at 5.2% for 2026-27 - higher than the 5% estimated earlier - to account for price pressure due to weather disruptions, weak monsoon and high volatility in international oil prices.
Crude oil prices are hovering above $100 (£75.33) a barrel resulting in India having to pay even more as the rupee has fallen close to its all-time lows against the dollar. The country imports around 90% of its crude oil and 50% of its gas needs.
The RBI last raised rates in February 2023, marking the end of its post-pandemic tightening cycle. During most of 2025, it cut rates to support economic growth before keeping policy unchanged from December 2025 until today's increase.
The rate increase is in line with expectations of economists who say that rising inflation makes a compelling case for it, especially since the economy has displayed enough resilience to absorb its impact without hurting growth.
It's also in line with what's happening globally. The US Federal Reserve has aggressively increased rates since 2022 pushing treasury bond yields higher. This, coupled with a strong dollar, has prompted investors to pull money from emerging markets such as India in search of higher returns in dollar assets.
On Wednesday, the RBI also upgraded its growth outlook after the economy outperformed expectations in the first quarter - the gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the current financial year is projected at 7.1%, up by 40 basis points from earlier estimate.
Governor Malhotra said the RBI would "strive for price and financial stability as both are essential for sustainable growth in the long run".
The RBI also signalled that it would use a mix of liquidity management tools to keep liquidity in check, while continuing to curb excessive volatility in the rupee.
Anuj Puri, chairman of real estate consulting firm ANAROCK Group, said the RBI rate hike may put pressure on consumer sentiment and discretionary spending. "The festive season is a key period for housing demand, and an increase in borrowing costs will affect buyer sentiment," he said.

All participants at the Federal Reserve's (Fed) September 15–16 meeting supported the 25-basis-point rate increase, while most judged that another hike would probably be appropriate by the end of the year. The Minutes show policymakers increasingly focused on upside inflation risks, a resilient economy and the possibility that strong AI investment could add to demand pressures.
Participants generally agreed that inflation remained elevated, while the labour market was close to full employment. Almost all saw inflation risks tilted to the upside, with some saying those risks had become more pronounced recently. Job-market risks were viewed as broadly balanced, giving the Fed greater scope to concentrate on restoring price stability.
Several officials warned that the AI buildout could eventually push aggregate demand ahead of supply, creating additional upward pressure on prices. The staff’s economic outlook was also stronger than in July, reinforcing the view that the economy could withstand further policy tightening. Against that backdrop, most participants considered another rate increase by year-end likely to be appropriate.
Financial conditions were also judged to remain supportive of growth despite the recent rise in long-term Treasury yields. A few participants said the Treasury market was functioning smoothly, while they stressed the importance of preparing for episodes of market stress.
Overall, the minutes reinforce a hawkish policy bias: the September hike was supported unanimously, and further tightening remained the most likely path if inflation fails to moderate.

This section below was published as a preview of the FOMC Minutes of the September 16-17 meeting at 16:30 GMT.
- The Fed Minutes are expected to shed some light on the extent and the timing of the monetary tightening cycle.
- Lower-than-expected price pressure and disappointing employment data have curbed hopes of back-to-back rate hikes.
- Futures market prices in a 20% chance of a rate hike in October and an 80% chance of at least one hike before year-end.
The United States (US) Federal Reserve (Fed) will release the Minutes of September’s Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Wednesday. Investors are eager for some details that shed light on the extent and the timing of the central bank´s tightening cycle after approving the first interest rate hike in three years in September.
The FOMC met expectations and raised the fed funds rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range in September in a unanimous decision. Chair Kevin Warsh surprised with unequivocally hawkish rhetoric, considering his natural reluctance to give excessive forward guidance. This reaffirmed investors’ confidence in the bank’s independence and sent the US Dollar rallying across the board.
Warsh stated that inflation has been “too high for too long” in the press conference following the decision. The monetary policy statement endorsed that view and reaffirmed the committee’s commitment to deliver price stability and pursue a monetary policy to “support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2% target.”
The statement also highlighted the strength of the US labour market, which boosted expectations of back-to-back rate hikes. Data released last week, however, has tempered those hopes, and investors will be analysing the Minutes to confirm a rate hike in December after practically discarding a tightening move later this month.
Inflation and labour data have dampened hopes of an October rate hike
US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Prices Index revealed that inflation remained steady in August, providing some leeway for the bank to take some time to better assess the impact of September’s rate hike before tightening monetary policy further. Beyond that, September’s Nonfarm Payrolls data has raised some doubts about the strength of the labour market altogether, strengthening the case for a pause at the next meeting.
Economic activity, however, remains solid. The US ISM Services Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) Index slowed down but remains at levels consistent with a strong expansion of business activity, reflecting strong demand and an improvement in employment. Data by GDPNow estimates that the US economy accelerated to 3.7% annual growth in the third quarter from the 2.2% increase seen in the previous quarter, providing an ideal scenario for a tightening cycle.
The question, thus, is on the timing, especially after mixed messages by Fed officials. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee affirmed last week that inflation outweighs labour market concerns at this moment, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan stated that more rate hikes will be needed to bring inflation to target. The central bank’s Vice Chair for Supervision, Michelle Bowman, on the other hand, said that there is not an urgent need for further rate hikes this year, and New York Fed President John Williams supported that idea.
Analysts at ING describe the latest data as slightly hawkish “but not enough to materially alter the Fed narrative.” In their view, “markets are likely to remain comfortable with an October hold provided September core CPI (released on 14 October) prints at 0.2% MoM, which is where consensus is converging.” ING reiterates that “a hike in December remains the base case,” keeping risks for the Dollar (USD) skewed to the upside.
When will FOMC Minutes be released, and how could they affect the US Dollar?
The FOMC will release the Minutes of its September 15-16 monetary policy meeting on Wednesday at 18:00 GMT.
The bank hiked interest rates by a quarter point and hinted at further rate hikes ahead, but recent data has dampened hopes of back-to-back rate hikes. Data from the CME’s FedWatch Tool shows a 78% chance that the bank will leave rates unchanged later this month, up from 50% last week. Hopes of some hike before the year-end, however, remain practically unchanged around an 85% chance.
Fed tightening hopes, combined with the US economic exceptionalism, concerns about high Oil prices that are weighing on most of the US Dollar’s rival currencies and, above all, a bond rout that has put the focus on the Euro Area, have propelled the US Dollar since early September. The US Dollar Index (DXY), which measures the value of the US Dollar against six majors, has rallied about 3.4% over the last four weeks to hit 18-month highs at 102.50.
Within this framework, the market expects the September Minutes to confirm that inflation remains front and center in the bank’s monetary policy plans, which would add to the case for a December hike.
The impact on the US Dollar, however, is likely to be limited as the report predates last week’s Personal Consumption Expenditures (Prices Index) and Nonfarm Payrolls reports. In that sense, next week’s US Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Producer Price Index (PPI) releases might have a higher impact, as they may set the outcome of the next meeting.
The daily chart shows the US Dollar Index (DXY) in a steady upward channel from early September lows, although the overbought Relative Strength Index (RSI) suggests that a consolidation or even some pullback should be considered. The Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) remains at positive levels, which suggests that dips are likely to find buyers.
DXY bulls have met resistance at the 127.7% Fibonacci retracement of the July-August bearish cycle in the 102.50 area. Further up, a previous support-turned-resistance at the 103.20 area (March 2025 lows) is likely to offer some resistance ahead of the 161.8% Fibonacci resistance of the mentioned cycle, at the 103.60 area.
Downside attempts so far are contained above previous year-to-date highs near the 101.80 area. A bearish reaction below that level would bring the September 25 low, at the 100.90 area, into focus, ahead of the psychological 100 level.

high_priority_articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03059-2Most LLMs cannot reliably evaluate text on the level of individual letters. A technique called byteification retrofits existing models to enable it.
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- NEWS AND VIEWS
Retrofitted LLM can count the letter ‘i’s in ‘artificial intelligence’
Strawberry contains the letter ‘r’ three times, but when asked, many large language models (LLMs) answer that the letter appears twice. This happens because most LLMs encode words as ‘tokens’ that represent sequences of letters. LLMs that operate in this way can achieve excellent performance, but they cannot access the individual characters in each word, which are encoded as binary sequences called bytes. Writing in Nature, Minixhofer et al.1 now report an approach called byteification that retrofits token-based LLMs to operate at the byte level. The authors show that byteified models can achieve competitive performance while retaining the ability to read individual characters.

South Pole, Gaïago and Gold Standard have issued the first carbon credits from a European regenerative agriculture programme covering farms in France and Belgium.
The issuance comes from the European Soil Revitalization Programme and covers its first 6,000 verified hectares. It is the first project globally to be design-certified and issue credits under Gold Standard’s Soil Organic Carbon Framework Methodology.
For corporate carbon buyers, the development opens a new source of verified removals in a sector where measurement and durability have often complicated investment.
Scaling soil carbon across European farms
The programme launched in 2022 and has a 20-year operational horizon. It currently brings together 727 farms across France and Belgium.
Once fully enrolled, the initiative will cover more than 39,282 hectares. It is forecast to remove 264,174 metric tons of CO₂ equivalent during its first crediting period.
Gaïago implements and operates the programme on the ground. South Pole has served as its carbon asset development partner since 2022. Its role includes project development and the verification processes needed to secure Gold Standard certification.
Farmers receive tailored support to introduce regenerative agricultural practices. These include reduced or zero tillage, which limits soil disturbance, and expanded year-round cover cropping. The practices are intended to increase soil carbon while improving water retention, nutrient levels and resilience.
Participants must also apply Gaïago’s NUTRIGEO L biostimulant. The product is designed to restore microbial diversity and improve soil structure.
The programme uses the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s GSOC MRV protocol and aligns with the FAO RECSOIL Initiative. So far, 1,972 local stakeholders have received training on soil health.
Carbon finance meets agricultural transition risk
Agricultural soils offer significant potential for carbon sequestration, but shifting farming practices can expose producers to financial and operational risks.
Carbon finance can help absorb some of those costs. For buyers, however, soil projects must demonstrate that claimed removals can be reliably measured and independently verified.
Aaron Barasz, Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operations Officer at South Pole, said: “Trust and integrity are non-negotiable for carbon credit buyers. This milestone proves that soil carbon removals can be measured, verified, and delivered at scale under the highest international standards. Drawing on over 20 years of carbon asset expertise, South Pole is proud to help corporate buyers invest with confidence in high-impact, future-proof, diversified removal strategies.”
Vanessa Pezet, Gaïago Carbon Program Director, said: “Transitioning to regenerative agriculture requires financial backing and practical support for farmers on the frontlines of climate change. As project proponent, Gaïago is showing that restoring soil health directly reinforces farmer resilience and productivity. This issuance validates the dedication of hundreds of French and Belgian farmers leading the agroecological transition.”

New option for corporate carbon buyers
The issuance arrives as corporate carbon strategies face tighter scrutiny over credit quality and the appropriate role of removals.
SBTi’s evolving Corporate Net-Zero Standard is particularly relevant. Its proposed approach gives carbon credits a defined role in addressing emissions as companies progress toward net zero, increasing attention on credible removal supply.
Sarah Leugers, Chief Growth Officer at Gold Standard, said: “Without healthy soil, life on our planet cannot thrive. It is not only a critical tool to mitigate emissions through carbon sequestration but also supports sustainable agriculture and global food security. As the first project worldwide to issue credits under our Soil Organic Carbon Framework Methodology, the European Soil Revitalization Programme shows how rigorous standards can unlock vital finance for sustainable land management. We congratulate Gaïago and South Pole on this important milestone.”
For investors and corporate buyers, the programme combines carbon removal with agricultural resilience and soil restoration. Its larger test will now be scale. If the model expands across its planned acreage while maintaining rigorous verification, it could strengthen Europe’s supply of land-based removals and channel more private climate finance directly into farming.
